sections.title: The vine that pulled the world to this coast
sections.intro_md:
Two thousand years ago a Roman ship called the **Hermapollon** sailed home from a port on the Kerala coast carrying pepper, ivory and fine cloth. A loan contract for that one cargo survives on a papyrus now in Vienna. The goods were worth about **9 million sesterces**, enough to buy a large estate in Italy.

The port was **Muziris**, and the thing everyone came for was **black pepper**, a vine that grows up the trunks of trees in the wet hills behind it. Romans, Arabs, Jews, Chinese and finally the Portuguese followed the smell. In May 1498 Vasco da Gama's ships anchored off Kozhikode and Europe's sea age in Asia began.

That is the paradox to keep in mind all day. Kerala is a thin strip of land, 1.2% of India, walled off by mountains. Yet it has always faced outwards, to the sea and to the world, and it still does: millions of Malayalis work abroad and send their earnings home.

spotlights.name: Black pepper

where.label: Western Ghats foothills, Idukki and Wayanad

spotlights.spot_it: A climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and hanging strings of green berries that turn red, then black when dried.
spotlights.story_md: Pepper is the dried fruit of *Piper nigrum*, a vine native to the Western Ghats. Pick the berries green, dry them in the sun for a week and they wrinkle and blacken: black pepper. Soak off the skin and you get white pepper. Rome was so hungry for it that when Alaric the Goth besieged the city in 408 CE, his ransom included 3,000 pounds of pepper, well over a tonne. Kerala farmers still grow it the old way, trained up jackfruit, mango or silver oak trees in home gardens.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Pepper made Kerala a node in world trade 1,500 years before the Portuguese arrived.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rome paid a Goth in pepper. Kerala grew the ransom.

spotlights.name: Muziris and Pattanam
spotlights.spot_it: Today: quiet fields and a small site museum near Kodungallur. Then: the busiest pepper port on the Indian Ocean.
spotlights.story_md: Greek and Tamil writers describe Muziris as a harbour crowded with Roman ships bringing gold to trade for pepper. Then it vanished. A great flood of the Periyar in **1341** is thought to have silted it up, and the same flood opened the harbour at Kochi. Since 2007 the Kerala Council for Historical Research has dug at **Pattanam**, finding Roman amphora shards, Mediterranean glass, a brick wharf with bollards and a six-metre canoe. Whether Pattanam is Muziris itself or a trading colony beside it is still argued.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The lost port explains why Kochi exists at all.
spotlights.memory_hook: One flood in 1341 killed a port and gave birth to another.

spotlights.name: Vasco da Gama at Kappad
spotlights.spot_it: A small white memorial stone under palms on a quiet beach north of Kozhikode.
spotlights.story_md: After ten months at sea Vasco da Gama reached the coast near **Kozhikode (Calicut)**, the city of the **Zamorin**, on 20 May 1498. When the first Portuguese man ashore was asked by two Tunisian traders what he wanted, he reportedly said: 'Christians and spices.' The Zamorin was unimpressed by Gama's gifts, which included striped cloth and hats. Gama came back in 1502 with warships and bombarded the city. He returned a third time as viceroy in 1524, fell ill and **died in Kochi on Christmas Eve 1524**. He was first buried in Kochi's St Francis Church; his remains went to Portugal in 1539.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It began 450 years of European power in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: He came for spices, left with them, and ended up buried in Kochi.

sections.title: Keralam at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Kerala runs about 580 km along India's south-west coast and is never more than about 120 km wide. The Western Ghats rise on its eastern edge, the Arabian Sea washes the west, and between them lie midland hills, rice paddies, 44 rivers and a maze of backwaters.

It was formed on **1 November 1956**, Kerala Piravi day, by joining the princely states of **Travancore** and **Kochi** with the **Malabar** district of the Madras Presidency. Since **25 August 2026** its official name is **Keralam**, the name Malayalis always used.

The numbers that matter: it is small and crowded, it has more women than men, it is the most literate large state, it has India's lowest share of multidimensionally poor people, and it is old: more than one Malayali in six is over 60. It sends more of its people abroad than almost any state, and their money has shaped everything from its houses to its politics.

spotlights.name: Kerala becomes Keralam
spotlights.spot_it: The white Victorian Secretariat in Thiruvananthapuram, seat of the state government since 1869.
spotlights.story_md: In Malayalam the state was always **Keralam**. The English and Hindi 'Kerala' stuck from colonial usage. The assembly asked for the change by unanimous resolution on 24 June 2024. The Union Cabinet approved it in February 2026, the Lok Sabha passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill on 11 August 2026 and the Rajya Sabha the next day. The gazette notification came on **25 August 2026**, just before Onam. The oldest written form of the name is older still: Ashoka's edicts in the 3rd century BCE mention the **Keralaputra**, the 'sons of Kerala', a Chera kingdom beyond his borders.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The new name is the first change to a state's name in over a decade.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ashoka wrote it first; Parliament spelt it right in 2026.

sections.title: The land: mountains, monsoon and land below the sea
sections.intro_md:
Kerala is three strips laid side by side. The **highlands** of the Western Ghats in the east hold forests, tea, cardamom and the state's peaks. The **midlands** are laterite hills with rubber, coconut and pepper. The **lowlands** along the coast are sand, lagoons and rice.

Water shapes everything. Kerala gets about **3,000 mm of rain a year**, most of it from the south-west monsoon, which reaches India first here, normally around **1 June**. In 2025 it arrived on **24 May**, the earliest since 2009. That rain fills 44 rivers, all short and fast, 41 of them flowing west to the sea.

Behind the coast, sandbars have trapped a chain of lagoons and canals, the **backwaters**, about 900 km of navigable water. The biggest, Vembanad, is the longest lake in India. Around it lies Kuttanad, where farmers grow rice below sea level.

spotlights.name: Anamudi and Eravikulam
spotlights.spot_it: A rounded, grassy summit shaped like an elephant's head, above rolling grassland and patches of dark shola forest.
spotlights.story_md: **Anamudi**, 'elephant's forehead', is 2,695 m high, the highest point in India south of the Himalaya. It stands in **Eravikulam National Park**, a high plateau of grassland and stunted shola forest near Munnar. The park was created mainly to protect the **Nilgiri tahr**, a wild mountain goat found only in the southern Western Ghats. Hunting and habitat loss pushed it close to extinction in the 20th century. Now Eravikulam holds the largest single population, and the tame tahr of the tourist zone will walk up to visitors on the road.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The roof of peninsular India, and the last fortress of an endemic goat.
spotlights.memory_hook: The highest point south of the Himalaya is an elephant's head with goats on it.

spotlights.name: Neelakurinji, the 12-year flower
spotlights.when: Mass bloom every 12 years; last 2018, next due 2030
spotlights.spot_it: Whole hillsides turned violet-blue by a small shrub in flower.
spotlights.story_md: *Strobilanthes kunthiana* grows across the high grasslands around Munnar and the Nilgiris. For eleven years it is an unremarkable shrub. In the twelfth, the plants flower together, then die, leaving seeds for the next cycle. The blooms of 2006 and **2018** turned the hills blue and drew huge crowds; the next mass bloom is expected around **2030**. The Muthuvan people of the hills have used the cycle to count age. The Nilgiris, the 'blue mountains', may take their name from it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare example of a plant that times its whole life to a 12-year clock.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blue hills once every twelve years: book now for 2030.

spotlights.name: Kuttanad: farming below the sea
spotlights.spot_it: Paddy fields lying visibly lower than the canal beside them, held back by mud bunds lined with coconut palms.
spotlights.story_md: **Kuttanad** is one of the few places on Earth where farmers grow rice **1 to 2 m below sea level**. From the 19th century they built bunds around shallow parts of **Vembanad Lake**, pumped them dry and planted rice in the lake bed. The fields, called padasekharams, are drained each season. The FAO named the system a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2013. The scientist M. S. Swaminathan, father of India's Green Revolution, traced his family to Kuttanad and championed it. The **Thanneermukkom bund** (1975) keeps salt water out in the dry season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the rice bowl of Kerala and a model for living with rising seas.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kerala's rice grows where the lake used to be.

spotlights.name: Silent Valley
spotlights.spot_it: Unbroken evergreen rainforest on steep slopes, said to be quiet because it lacks cicadas.
spotlights.story_md: In the 1970s the state planned a hydroelectric dam on the Kunthipuzha river that would have flooded one of India's last undisturbed tropical evergreen forests. Scientists, poets and a science movement, the **Kerala Sasthra Sahithya Parishad**, campaigned against it, and the **lion-tailed macaque**, a black monkey with a silver mane, became the face of the fight. Indira Gandhi's government shelved the project, and the area was declared a national park in **1984**. It was one of India's first big environmental victories, a decade before such fights were common.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved a development project could be stopped to save a forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A monkey with a lion's mane beat a dam.

sections.title: Stone carvings, Cheras and three faiths by sea
sections.intro_md:
People carved pictures into the rock of Wayanad thousands of years before any written record. By the time of the **Sangam** poems in Tamil (roughly 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE), the land was ruled by the **Cheras**, one of three great Tamil dynasties, and its ports traded with Rome. Malayalam had not yet split from Tamil.

What makes Kerala's early history unusual is that the world's religions arrived by ship, peacefully, and stayed. Christian tradition says the apostle **Thomas** landed at Muziris in 52 CE. Jewish traders were here by the first millennium; around 1000 CE a Chera king granted a Jewish leader, Joseph Rabban, privileges on copper plates. Arab traders brought Islam early, perhaps within its first century. A second Chera kingdom ruled from Mahodayapuram, near Kodungallur, from about 800 to 1124 CE, after which the land broke into small kingdoms: Kozhikode under the Zamorins, Kochi, Venad (later Travancore) and others.

spotlights.name: Edakkal Caves
spotlights.when: Carvings possibly Neolithic; inscriptions early centuries CE
spotlights.spot_it: A cleft in a boulder high on a hill, its walls scratched with stick figures, animals, wheels and headdressed people.
spotlights.story_md: Edakkal is not really a cave but a gap under a huge rock that split and wedged itself between two others; the name means 'a stone in between'. In 1890 the British police officer Fred Fawcett, out hunting, found its walls covered in **petroglyphs**: human figures with headdresses, animals, wheels, and a figure some read as a man with a jar. Their dating is debated, with estimates ranging from Neolithic times to the early centuries CE. Later visitors added inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi. A climb of a few hundred steps leads to it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The oldest art in Kerala, and among the oldest rock engravings in south India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A stone stuck in between, with Kerala's first drawings inside.

spotlights.name: Cheraman Juma Masjid
spotlights.when: Tradition: 629 CE; present building much later
spotlights.spot_it: A mosque that looks like a Kerala temple: sloping tiled roofs, wooden gables, a brass lamp, no dome.
spotlights.story_md: Local tradition says a Chera king, Cheraman Perumal, saw the moon split, sailed to Arabia, accepted Islam and sent letters home asking for a mosque to be built, and that this mosque was founded in **629 CE**, which would make it India's oldest. Historians treat the story as legend: the king's journey is not documented and the present building is much later. A 1970s concrete front was removed in a 2022 restoration that brought back the old Kerala form. It still keeps a traditional lamp lit, a temple custom, and people of all faiths visit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Islam in Kerala grew out of trade and local architecture, not conquest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mosque in a temple's clothes, with a moon-splitting legend.

spotlights.name: Paradesi Synagogue
spotlights.spot_it: A small white synagogue with a clock tower at the end of a street of spice shops; inside, blue Chinese tiles and Belgian chandeliers.
spotlights.story_md: Built in **1568** next to the Kochi raja's palace, which gave the land, it is the oldest active synagogue in the Commonwealth. 'Paradesi' means foreigners: it was built by Jews who came from Spain, Portugal and the Middle East, as distinct from the much older Malabari Jews. In the 1760s a merchant laid a floor of about 1,100 **hand-painted Canton tiles**, no two said to be identical. Its clock tower has faces in Hebrew, Malayalam and Roman numerals. Most of Kochi's Jews emigrated to Israel after 1948; only a handful remain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two thousand years of Jewish life in Kerala, almost without persecution, ends here.
spotlights.memory_hook: A clock that tells time in three scripts, in a town almost empty of its people.

spotlights.name: Saint Thomas Christians
spotlights.when: Tradition: 52 CE; documented by the 6th century
spotlights.spot_it: Ancient churches with Kerala-style gables and stone crosses; families named Mathew, Thomas, Kurian who call themselves Nasranis.
spotlights.story_md: Kerala's oldest Christians trace their faith to **St Thomas the Apostle**, who tradition says landed at Muziris in 52 CE and founded seven churches, Palayur among them. The tradition cannot be proven, but a Christian community linked to the Church of the East was here by the 6th century. They worshipped in Syriac and lived as a high-status trading caste. When the Portuguese pushed them under Rome, thousands gathered at a cross in Mattancherry in **1653** and swore the **Coonan Cross Oath**, holding a rope tied to the cross. The split it began still shapes Kerala's many churches.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Kerala had Christians long before Europe reached India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rope tied to a cross split a church in 1653.

sections.title: Travancore, reform and the road to one state
sections.intro_md:
In 1729 a young ruler, **Marthanda Varma**, began turning the small southern kingdom of Venad into **Travancore**, swallowing his neighbours and beating a European power. By the 19th century Travancore was a model princely state with schools, a modern bureaucracy and, in 1817, a royal order for free and compulsory education under Rani Gowri Parvathi Bayi.

It was also one of the most caste-bound societies in India. Lower castes could not use certain roads, had to keep set distances from Brahmins and, for some, women were forbidden to cover their upper bodies. The century from 1850 to 1950 is the story of how that system was broken from below: by the **Channar revolt** over the right to wear an upper cloth, by **Sree Narayana Guru**, by **Ayyankali**, by the **Vaikom Satyagraha** and finally by the **Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936**.

After independence Travancore and Kochi merged in 1949. In 1956 Malabar joined them, and Kerala was born.

spotlights.name: Battle of Colachel

where.label: Colachel, now Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu

spotlights.spot_it: A painting at Padmanabhapuram Palace shows a Dutch officer kneeling in surrender before the Travancore king.
spotlights.story_md: In 1741 the Dutch East India Company landed troops at Colachel to bully Travancore over pepper. Marthanda Varma's army trapped and defeated them on **10 August 1741**. It is often called the first defeat of a European naval power by an Indian kingdom. One prisoner, a Flemish officer named **Eustachius De Lannoy**, switched sides and modernised Travancore's army for 36 years, building the Udayagiri fort where he is buried. A victory pillar stands at Colachel; the town has been in Tamil Nadu since 1956.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended Dutch ambitions in Kerala and made Travancore a regional power.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Dutch lost a battle and Travancore gained their general.

spotlights.name: Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A seven-tier stone gopuram over a temple tank, in the heart of the capital; men in mundu, women in sari only.
spotlights.story_md: Inside, Vishnu reclines on the serpent Anantha in an 18-ft image made of **12,008 saligram stones**, seen in parts through three doors. In **1750** Marthanda Varma gave his whole kingdom to the deity and ruled as **Padmanabha Dasa**, the god's servant; Thiruvananthapuram means 'city of the sacred serpent'. In **2011**, on Supreme Court orders, inspectors opened the temple's underground vaults and found gold coins, jewels and idols worth, by widely reported estimates, over **₹1 lakh crore**. One vault, **B**, has not been opened. In 2020 the Supreme Court upheld the royal family's role in running the temple.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Possibly the richest place of worship on Earth, and still sealed in part.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king gave his kingdom to a god; the god kept the gold in the basement.

spotlights.name: Vaikom Satyagraha
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of men in white walking in pairs towards police barricades on a temple road.
spotlights.story_md: Roads around the Shiva temple at Vaikom were closed to 'untouchable' castes. On **30 March 1924** volunteers, an Ezhava, a Pulaya and a Nair walking together, tried to use them and were arrested. Day after day for **more than 600 days** others followed, standing in floodwater when the 1924 rains came. Akali Sikhs from Punjab ran a free kitchen. **Periyar E. V. Ramasamy** came from Madras and was jailed twice, earning the name 'Vaikom Veerar'. Gandhi visited in 1925. The protest ended with three of the four roads opened to all.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first great organised fight against untouchability in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six hundred days to walk down one road.

spotlights.name: Sree Narayana Guru
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, calm man in white, often shown in meditation; his statue stands at junctions all over Kerala.
spotlights.story_md: Born into the Ezhava caste, which was barred from Brahmin temples, Narayana Guru did something radical in **1888** at **Aruvippuram**: he consecrated a Shiva idol himself. When challenged, he said he had installed an Ezhava Shiva. He later placed mirrors in temples instead of idols. His creed was **'One caste, one religion, one God for humankind'**, and he pushed education and industry: 'Liberate through education, strengthen through organisation.' The SNDP Yogam, founded in 1903 under his inspiration, remains one of Kerala's most powerful community bodies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned caste reform into a mass movement without violence.
spotlights.memory_hook: He put up a mirror and called it God.

spotlights.name: Ayyankali
spotlights.spot_it: A Dalit leader in a turban and coat; statues show him with a bullock cart.
spotlights.story_md: Pulayas, the agricultural labourers at the bottom of Travancore's order, could not walk public roads. In **1893** Ayyankali, a Pulaya, bought a bullock cart (a 'villuvandi'), dressed like a landlord and drove it down the forbidden roads of Venganoor. Later he organised what may be India's first farm workers' strike, refusing to work the fields until Pulaya children were admitted to school. In 1911 he was nominated to the Sree Moolam Popular Assembly of Travancore.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He won Dalits the right to roads and schools by force of will.
spotlights.memory_hook: One man, one bullock cart, one forbidden road.

sections.title: The Kerala model: rich in health, modest in income
sections.intro_md:
In the 1970s economists noticed something odd. Kerala's income per person was below India's average, yet its people lived as long, read as well and lost as few babies as people in much richer countries. They called it the **Kerala model**.

The roots go back to the education orders of Travancore and Kochi, the reform movements, missionaries, and then to politics. In **1957** Kerala elected a communist government, which pushed land reform and schooling. Governments of the left (LDF) and the Congress-led front (UDF) have alternated almost every five years since, and both kept spending on schools, primary health care and food rations. Kerala was declared fully literate on **18 April 1991**.

The model has costs. Kerala has high unemployment among educated young people, among the highest public debt ratios in India, high rates of diabetes and an ageing population. Much of its prosperity comes from money sent home by workers abroad.

spotlights.name: E. M. S. Namboodiripad and the 1957 government
spotlights.spot_it: A slight man with glasses and a stammer, a Brahmin landlord's son who became Kerala's first Chief Minister.
spotlights.story_md: EMS gave away much of his family's property to the Communist Party. On **5 April 1957** his party took office after winning a state election, one of the first elected communist governments anywhere. It passed an education bill to regulate private schools and a land bill to protect tenants. Churches, the Nair Service Society and the Congress launched a mass agitation, the **Vimochana Samaram** ('liberation struggle'), and on **31 July 1959** the Centre dismissed the government under Article 356. EMS became Chief Minister again in 1967.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set Kerala's political pattern: left and centre trading power, both pursuing welfare.
spotlights.memory_hook: Elected in 1957, dismissed in 1959, imitated ever since.

spotlights.name: Land to the tiller
spotlights.when: Land Reforms Act 1963, in force 1 January 1970
spotlights.spot_it: K. R. Gouri Amma, the revenue minister who drafted it, in a white sari in old age.
spotlights.story_md: **K. R. Gouri Amma** (1919 to 2021), one of the first women lawyers from the Ezhava community, was revenue minister in 1957 and drafted the Agrarian Relations Bill. After years of court battles, the **Kerala Land Reforms Act** came fully into force on **1 January 1970**: tenancy was abolished and some 1.5 million tenant households became owners of the land they farmed, or of the plot under their hut. Gouri Amma lived to 102, was a minister in six governments and was expelled from the party she helped build.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Kerala's land reform was one of the most thorough in any democracy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lawyer's bill turned tenants into owners.

spotlights.name: Kudumbashree
spotlights.spot_it: Ten to twenty women sitting on a floor with a ledger, at a weekly neighbourhood group meeting.
spotlights.story_md: Kudumbashree ('prosperity of the family') is a state poverty programme built from small neighbourhood groups of women, linked into ward and village federations. Members pool savings, give each other small loans and run businesses: canteens, catering for government offices, farms, tailoring, cleaning crews, even the state's lottery sales counters. It has more than **45 lakh** members, roughly one woman in every two households. Its 'Janakeeya hotels' sell meals for about ₹20 to ₹30.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest women's networks in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kerala's biggest women's movement meets on the floor once a week.

sections.title: Malayalam and the Kerala school
sections.intro_md:
About 97% of Keralites speak **Malayalam**, a Dravidian language that grew out of the western dialects of old Tamil, separating fully by around the 9th to 13th centuries and absorbing a great deal of Sanskrit. It has about 35 million speakers and was declared a **classical language** of India in 2013. Its name is a palindrome in English letters, a fact every Malayali child is told.

The script is rounded, partly because it was scratched onto palm leaves with an iron stylus, where straight lines would split the leaf. Early Malayalam literature mixed Tamil and Sanskrit forms; the 16th century poet **Ezhuthachan** set the modern literary language.

Kerala also produced one of the great schools of medieval mathematics. Between the 14th and 16th centuries, scholars in villages along the Nila river found infinite series for pi and for sine and cosine, results Europe reached two to three centuries later.

spotlights.name: The Malayalam script
spotlights.spot_it: Letters made almost entirely of loops and curves, with few straight strokes.
spotlights.story_md: Malayalam is written in a Brahmi-derived script that grew from Grantha, used to write Sanskrit in the south. Its round shapes suit palm-leaf writing. The first book printed with Malayalam letters was not printed in India: it was **Hortus Malabaricus**, a 12-volume Latin flora of Kerala's plants compiled by the Dutch governor Hendrik van Rheede with Ezhava physician **Itty Achuden** and published in Amsterdam from 1678. The script was simplified in 1971 for typewriters and printing, and digital fonts have since brought back many of the older joined letters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A distinct script helped make Malayalam a separate language, not a dialect.
spotlights.memory_hook: Round letters, because straight lines would tear the leaf.

spotlights.name: Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan
spotlights.spot_it: Thunchan Parambu in Tirur, where on Vijayadashami children write their first letters in a plate of rice.
spotlights.story_md: Ezhuthachan, 'father of letters', is called the father of modern Malayalam. His **Adhyatma Ramayanam Kilippattu** retells the Ramayana as if sung by a parrot (kili), in plain Malayalam that ordinary people could follow. During the monsoon month of Karkidakam, many Hindu homes in Kerala still read a part of it every evening. On **Vidyarambham**, the day of learning in the Navaratri season, thousands of small children are brought to his birthplace at Tirur to trace their first letters in rice, with sand taken from the site prized as a blessing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made Malayalam a language for literature, not just for speech.
spotlights.memory_hook: A parrot taught Kerala to read the Ramayana.

spotlights.name: Madhava and the Kerala school
spotlights.spot_it: No portrait survives; the evidence is palm-leaf manuscripts in Sanskrit and Malayalam.
spotlights.story_md: **Madhava of Sangamagrama** (about 1340 to 1425) found that pi can be written as an endless sum: 1 minus 1/3 plus 1/5 minus 1/7 and so on, times four. Europe credits this to Leibniz and Gregory in the 1670s. Madhava also found series for sine and cosine and used them to compute pi to 11 decimal places. His successors **Nilakantha Somayaji** (Tantrasangraha, 1500) and **Jyeshthadeva** wrote it up; Jyeshthadeva's **Yuktibhasa** (about 1530) gives proofs, in Malayalam. Whether the ideas reached Europe through Jesuits in Kochi is a theory without direct evidence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is calculus-style mathematics, 250 years before Newton, in a Kerala village.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pi as an infinite sum was a Kerala discovery first.

sections.title: Temples, shrines and gods who dance
sections.intro_md:
In Census 2011, Kerala was **54.7% Hindu, 26.6% Muslim and 18.4% Christian**, the most religiously mixed of the large states. All three faiths have lived side by side for over a thousand years, and they share a building language: tiled roofs, lamps, processions, elephants, drums.

Kerala's Hindu temples look different from those elsewhere in the south. Most are low, with sloping copper or tiled roofs, a round or square sanctum and a tall brass lamp pillar outside, and dress codes are strict. Temple arts, from Koodiyattam to the drum orchestras of the festivals, grew in their courtyards.

Alongside the great temples runs an older layer: sacred groves (kavu) for snakes and local goddesses, and in north Kerala the **theyyam**, where a performer becomes a god for a night.

spotlights.name: Sabarimala
spotlights.spot_it: Men in black or saffron mundus with a cloth bundle (irumudi) on their heads, climbing a forest hill chanting 'Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa'.
spotlights.story_md: The hill shrine of **Ayyappa** in the forests of the Periyar Tiger Reserve draws millions of pilgrims in each Mandala-Makaravilakku season. Pilgrims keep a **41-day vow**: no meat, alcohol or sex, sleeping on the floor, wearing black. They climb the 18 holy steps carrying a two-part bundle with a ghee-filled coconut. By custom women aged 10 to 50 did not go. In **2018** the Supreme Court ruled that ban unconstitutional; massive protests followed, very few women entered, and in 2019 the court sent the wider question to a larger bench, where it still sits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the largest annual pilgrimages in the world, and India's biggest faith-versus-equality case.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty-one days of discipline for eighteen steps.

spotlights.name: Guruvayur and its elephants
spotlights.spot_it: A Krishna temple thronged with wedding parties; a short drive away, dozens of elephants chained under trees at Punnathur Kotta.
spotlights.story_md: Guruvayur is Kerala's most popular Krishna temple, and dozens of weddings can take place outside it on an auspicious morning. Devotees have long donated elephants to the deity, and the temple keeps more than 30 of them at **Punnathur Kotta**, an old palace grounds turned elephant camp. The 1931 **Guruvayur Satyagraha** fought for entry of lower castes; the temple only opened to all Hindus in 1947. Non-Hindus are still not allowed inside, a rule that has kept even the famous singer K. J. Yesudas, a Christian, outside.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Kerala's temple economy, elephants and caste history all meet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Krishna owns a herd of elephants.

spotlights.name: Attukal Pongala
spotlights.spot_it: Women, side by side for kilometres along the city's roads, cooking sweet rice in clay pots on bricks over small fires.
spotlights.story_md: On one day each year the streets of Thiruvananthapuram fill with women cooking **pongala**, rice with jaggery and coconut, as an offering to the goddess of the Attukal temple. A flame lit inside the temple is passed from hearth to hearth across the city. **Guinness** recorded about **1.5 million** women in 1997 and **2.5 million** in 2009, the largest gathering of women for a religious event. Reports put 2026's crowd, on 3 March, near **40 lakh**. Men are not barred but the day belongs to women; the city fire service and volunteers stand by.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest single gathering of women in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city-sized kitchen, lit from one flame.

spotlights.name: Theyyam
spotlights.spot_it: A performer with a red-and-black painted face, silver eye ornaments and a towering headdress, dancing by firelight in a village shrine.
spotlights.story_md: In north Malabar, gods visit in person. A **theyyam** performer, usually from a Dalit or backward community such as the Malayan, Vannan or Pulayar, spends hours being painted and dressed, looks into a mirror, and becomes the deity. For that night upper-caste landlords bow to him and ask for blessings. There are said to be more than **400 theyyams**, including deified heroes, ancestors and women wronged in life. Some performers walk through fire; Muchilottu Bhagavathi's headdress can be several metres tall. Next morning the god is a labourer again.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It inverts caste for a night and preserves stories nowhere written down.
spotlights.memory_hook: By night a god, by day a daily-wage worker.

sections.title: Kathakali, Koodiyattam and the warrior's pit
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's stage is built on the face. Its great dance-dramas use make-up as a code, so an audience knows a character's nature before he moves, and they train the eyes as hard as the feet: Kathakali students practise eye exercises daily for years.

The oldest form, **Koodiyattam**, is Sanskrit theatre performed in temple theatres for at least a thousand years. **Kathakali** grew from it and from Krishnanattam in the 17th century. **Mohiniyattam**, the solo 'dance of the enchantress', is its gentle counterpart. Many of these arts survived the 20th century because the poet **Vallathol Narayana Menon** founded **Kerala Kalamandalam** in 1930 to teach them.

The martial art **Kalaripayattu** sits behind all of them. Kathakali's leaps, stances and massage regime come from the kalari. And everything is driven by the **chenda**, a cylindrical drum loud enough to be heard across a festival ground.

spotlights.name: Kathakali
spotlights.spot_it: Green painted face framed by a white ridged paper 'chutti', huge billowing skirt, crown, long silver nails; red eyes.
spotlights.story_md: In Kathakali, colour tells you who is who. **Pacha** (green) is the noble hero, like Krishna or Arjuna. **Kathi** (knife) is the proud villain, green with red marks and white knobs on nose and forehead. **Thadi** (beard) means red for evil, white for divine, black for hunters. **Minukku** (polished) is for women and sages. The make-up takes three to four hours, and actors put a seed in their eyes to turn them red. Performances once ran from dusk to dawn, lit by a single brass lamp. Actors do not speak: singers behind them sing the text while the actor acts it with 24 basic hand gestures.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the most demanding acting disciplines in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Green for good, red beard for evil, and a seed in the eye.

compare.difference: Kathakali is a male, masked, thunderous dance-drama; Mohiniyattam is a solo female dance of swaying grace.

spotlights.name: Mohiniyattam
spotlights.spot_it: A solo dancer in a white sari with a gold border, hair in a bun on the left side, swaying gently like a palm in the wind.
spotlights.story_md: Mohiniyattam, 'dance of Mohini', the enchantress form of Vishnu, is all lasya: soft, circular, swaying movement of the torso, with the feet kept close to the ground. It was refined at the Travancore court under the composer-king **Swathi Thirunal** in the 1800s, then fell into disrepute and was nearly lost. Vallathol brought it into Kalamandalam in the 1930s, and dancers such as **Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma** rebuilt it. The costume, white and gold kasavu, is Kerala's festival dress.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It kept a female classical tradition alive in Kerala.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kathakali thunders; Mohiniyattam sways.

spotlights.name: Koodiyattam
spotlights.spot_it: An actor on a small temple stage, a huge mizhavu drum behind him, taking twenty minutes to show a single flower opening with his eyes.
spotlights.story_md: Koodiyattam ('acting together') is the oldest surviving theatre in India, staging Sanskrit plays with Malayalam commentary. It was performed by the Chakyar community, with Nangiar women playing female roles, inside **koothambalams**, theatres within temples. A single act can take days, and a full play can run for **up to 41 nights**, because the actor elaborates every word. In **2001** it became the first Indian art proclaimed a **UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living link to Sanskrit drama as it was actually staged.
spotlights.memory_hook: A play that takes 41 nights.

spotlights.name: Kalaripayattu
spotlights.when: Medieval; codified by the 12th century or earlier
spotlights.spot_it: Fighters in a red-earth pit leaping with swords, shields, sticks and a flexible sword called urumi that whips like a belt.
spotlights.story_md: Kalaripayattu is trained in a **kalari**, a sunken pit with a shrine in one corner. Students begin with years of body work, kicks, leaps and animal stances, oiled and massaged to stay supple, then move to sticks, daggers, swords and the urumi. Masters (gurukkal) also learn **marma**, the vital points of the body, both to strike and to heal. The art was suppressed under British rule and revived in the 1920s. **Meenakshi Amma** of Vatakara, still teaching in her seventies, was given the Padma Shri in 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It feeds Kerala's dance, medicine and cinema, and claims a place among the oldest martial arts.
spotlights.memory_hook: Learn to heal the point before you learn to strike it.

spotlights.name: Chenda melam
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of men with tall cylindrical drums slung at the hip, striking with curved sticks, cymbals and horns behind them.
spotlights.story_md: The **chenda** is a cylindrical wooden drum with skins at both ends, played with sticks, and it is famously loud. A **melam** is an ensemble of chendas with ilathalam cymbals and kombu horns. The **Panchari melam** slowly speeds up through five stages over hours. At Thrissur Pooram, the **Ilanjithara melam** under a tree inside the Vadakkunnathan temple has more than 200 drummers playing to tens of thousands. Kerala calls the chenda the 'asura vadyam', the demon instrument, because it drowns everything else.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the heartbeat of every Kerala festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: The demon instrument wins every argument.

sections.title: Murals, a painter of gods and a mirror without glass
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's visual arts begin on temple and palace walls. From about the 16th century painters covered them with **murals** in five natural colours, crowded with gods whose eyes and ornaments are drawn with obsessive care. The best surviving sets are in **Mattancherry Palace** in Kochi and **Padmanabhapuram Palace**.

In the 19th century a Travancore aristocrat, **Raja Ravi Varma**, learned European oil painting and used it to paint Indian gods and heroines. His printed copies decided what Indian gods look like to this day.

The crafts are about materials Kerala has in abundance: bell metal, wood, coconut. Coconut fibre, **coir**, became an industry. A family of metalworkers in one village still makes a mirror of polished metal by a formula they keep to themselves.

spotlights.name: Kerala murals
spotlights.spot_it: Wall paintings in ochre, red, green, yellow and black, packed edge to edge with many-armed gods, long eyes and jewelled crowns.
spotlights.story_md: Kerala murals use a fixed palette, **panchavarna**, five colours made from minerals and plants: red and yellow ochre, green from a plant leaf, white from lime and black from lamp soot. Figures are outlined, then filled, then given fine ornament. The 16th century Ramayana panels at **Mattancherry Palace**, built by the Portuguese for the Kochi raja in 1555, cover entire rooms. The tradition nearly died in the 20th century; Guruvayur's Institute of Mural Painting, set up in 1989, now trains painters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A distinct Indian school of wall painting, still being practised.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five colours, endless jewellery.

spotlights.name: Raja Ravi Varma
spotlights.spot_it: Oil paintings of Indian women in draped saris with soft, realistic faces, and gods who look like Indian aristocrats.
spotlights.story_md: Born into a noble family at Kilimanoor, Ravi Varma learned oils by watching a Dutch-trained painter at the Travancore court. He painted scenes from the epics with European realism and Indian models. In **1894** he set up a lithographic press near Bombay and printed cheap colour **oleographs** of gods. Millions of homes hung them, and his Lakshmi and Saraswati shaped calendar art, film sets and the faces of Indian deities ever since. Critics later called him derivative; collectors now pay crores for his canvases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave India its standard image of its own gods.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every calendar goddess has his brushwork in her face.

spotlights.name: Aranmula kannadi
spotlights.spot_it: A round mirror in a brass frame that reflects from its front surface, so there is no double image at the edge.
spotlights.story_md: An ordinary mirror has silver behind glass. The **Aranmula kannadi** is a disc of **cast metal alloy**, mostly copper and tin, polished for days until it reflects. Because the image sits on the surface there is no ghost reflection. The exact alloy is a secret kept by a few families of the Vishwakarma community in the temple village of Aranmula. It is one of the 'ashtamangalyam', the eight auspicious objects in a Kerala bride's set, and it was given a **Geographical Indication** tag in 2004-05.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A craft secret kept inside one village for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mirror with no glass and no second face.

sections.title: Coconut, rice and fish: what Kerala eats
sections.intro_md:
Kerala cooks with **coconut**: grated, ground into paste, squeezed for milk, pressed for oil. The state's name may even come from 'kera', the coconut palm. Rice is eaten at every meal, often a fat red parboiled grain called matta. Fish curry, sour with **kudampuli** (Malabar tamarind), is the default.

Then the communities diverge. **Hindu** vegetarian feasts end in payasam. **Syrian Christian** kitchens make appam and stew, duck roast and beef fry. The **Mappila** Muslims of Malabar cook pathiri, biryani and snacks that show their Arab links. Kerala is one of the few states where beef is widely eaten across communities.

Snacks are a religion of their own: banana chips fried in coconut oil, pazham pori (banana fritters), and 'chaya' (tea) poured from a height at a roadside shop.

spotlights.name: Sadya
spotlights.spot_it: A banana leaf, tip pointing left, with rice in the middle and two dozen small dishes in fixed places around it.
spotlights.story_md: A sadya is a vegetarian feast of **20 to 28 dishes** served on a banana leaf, eaten with the right hand. Each dish has a set place: salt, banana chips and sharkara upperi at the top left, pickles next to them, then thoran, avial, olan, kalan, erissery; rice is served with parippu (dal) and ghee first, then sambar, then rasam, then **payasam**, often two or three kinds, then buttermilk to finish. The leaf is laid with its tip to the diner's left. At the end, many fold the leaf towards themselves to say the meal was good.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Kerala's grammar of food in one meal.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-six dishes, one leaf, one hand.

spotlights.name: Appam and stew
spotlights.spot_it: A bowl-shaped rice pancake, lacy and crisp at the edges, spongy in the centre, with a white coconut-milk stew.
spotlights.story_md: Appam is made from rice batter fermented overnight, traditionally with **toddy** (palm wine) or now yeast, swirled in a small rounded pan called an appachatti so it forms thin crisp edges and a thick soft middle. It is eaten with **stew** (ishtu), vegetables or chicken cooked gently in coconut milk with whole spices: a dish that shows Portuguese and Syrian Christian influences. It is Easter breakfast in many homes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A shared dish of Kerala's Christians that the whole state adopted.
spotlights.memory_hook: Toddy makes the lace.

spotlights.name: Karimeen pollichathu
spotlights.spot_it: A whole small fish wrapped in a charred banana leaf, opened to show red masala.
spotlights.story_md: **Karimeen**, the pearl spot (*Etroplus suratensis*), is a brackish-water fish of the backwaters. Kerala made it the **state fish** in 2010. For pollichathu it is marinated in chilli, shallots and kudampuli, wrapped in banana leaf and cooked on a hot pan until the leaf blackens and the fish steams inside. The best is eaten in the toddy shops and houseboats of Kuttanad and Kumarakom.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the taste of the backwaters.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kerala's state fish comes wrapped in a leaf.

spotlights.name: Toddy and the kallu shap
spotlights.spot_it: A man climbing a coconut palm with a pot at his waist; a small shop with a board saying 'kallu' by a canal.
spotlights.story_md: **Toddy** (kallu) is the sap of the coconut palm, collected by tappers who climb trees twice a day and cut the flower stalk. Left alone it ferments within hours into a mildly sour, mildly alcoholic drink. It is sold in licensed **toddy shops** (kallu shap), which are also some of Kerala's best places for spicy food: fish curry, duck roast, tapioca. Toddy tapping was a traditional occupation of the Ezhava caste, and Sree Narayana Guru urged his followers to give it up.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It links food, caste reform and the coconut economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: The palm makes the drink; the shop makes the fish curry.

sections.title: Onam, boats and elephants
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's year turns on the Malayalam calendar, the **Kollam era**, which began in 825 CE. **Onam**, in the month of Chingam (August to September), is the state festival for all communities. **Vishu**, the Malayali new year in April, starts with a sight. Between them come temple festivals with caparisoned elephants, church feasts with processions, Muslim nerchas, and the boat races of the monsoon season.

The two biggest spectacles are on the water and in the temple grounds: the **snake boat races** of Alappuzha and **Thrissur Pooram**, where two temples compete with elephants, parasols and drums. Both are tests of teamwork as much as faith.

spotlights.name: Onam
spotlights.spot_it: A circle of flower petals at every doorstep, growing ring by ring over ten days; men painted as tigers dancing in Thrissur.
spotlights.story_md: Onam welcomes home **Mahabali**, a demon king so just that the gods grew jealous. Vishnu came as a dwarf, Vamana, asked for three steps of land and pushed him into the underworld, but granted him one visit a year. Over ten days from Atham to **Thiruvonam**, families build a **pookalam** (flower carpet), wear new clothes (onakkodi), play games and eat the sadya. In Thrissur on the fourth day, **Pulikali** dancers painted as tigers and hunters dance through the streets with their bellies made up as tiger faces.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The shared festival of a religiously mixed state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A good king visits once a year; Kerala dresses the doorstep.

spotlights.name: Snake boat races
spotlights.when: Nehru Trophy since 1952, second Saturday of August
spotlights.spot_it: A boat over 30 m long and barely wider than a man, with a high curved stern, dozens of oars flashing in time, a singer keeping rhythm.
spotlights.story_md: A **chundan vallam** (snake boat) is 30 to 42 m long and carries around 100 people: about 90 rowers, helmsmen with long oars at the stern, and singers. Each belongs to a village, which worships it like a temple deity. In **1952** Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru watched a race at Alappuzha, was so excited he jumped into the winning boat, and later sent a silver trophy. The **Nehru Trophy** has been rowed on Punnamada Lake ever since. Since 2019 a **Champions Boat League** has turned the races into a season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest team sport on water in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred oars, one village, one boat.

spotlights.name: Thrissur Pooram
spotlights.spot_it: Two lines of caparisoned elephants facing each other, men on their backs flipping parasols in sequence while a crowd roars.
spotlights.story_md: In **1798** the Kochi ruler **Sakthan Thampuran** brought together ten temples around Thrissur's Vadakkunnathan temple into one festival. Two sides, **Paramekkavu** and **Thiruvambadi**, compete. The climax is **Kudamattam**: some 15 elephants on each side face each other while the men on top switch between dozens of sets of brilliantly coloured parasols, each side trying to outshine the other. Before it the Ilanjithara melam plays for hours; after midnight comes a huge fireworks display.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Kerala's biggest temple festival, and a test of design one-upmanship.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two temples, thirty elephants, a parasol war.

sections.title: How Kerala lives: houses, the Gulf and football
sections.intro_md:
Many old rules have flipped in Kerala within a lifetime. Several communities, above all the **Nairs**, once followed **matrilineal** inheritance: property passed through women and a household was run by the mother's eldest brother. That system was abolished by law in 1975-76, and today's family is nuclear and often spread across continents.

The great modern force is **migration**. From the 1970s oil boom, Malayalis went in huge numbers to the Gulf as labourers, nurses, drivers and accountants. The Kerala Migration Surveys put emigrants at roughly **2 million** in recent years, with remittances above ₹2 lakh crore in 2023. Big 'Gulf houses' in villages, empty for much of the year, and an older generation living alone are the visible results. Students are the new emigrants, heading to Canada, the UK, Australia and Europe.

Public life is intensely political and literate: newspapers such as **Malayala Manorama** (1888) and **Mathrubhumi** (1923) are among India's biggest, and tea-shop arguments are a pastime. So is football.

spotlights.name: Tharavad and nalukettu
spotlights.spot_it: A large old house of wood and laterite with sloping tiled roofs built around an open courtyard that catches the rain.
spotlights.story_md: Among Nairs and some other communities, the **tharavad** (joint family house) followed **marumakkathayam**: descent and property through the female line. Children belonged to their mother's family, and the karanavar, the mother's eldest brother, managed the estate. The classic house was a **nalukettu**, four blocks around a central courtyard (nadumuttam) open to the sky. Laws from 1925 onward let members split the property, and the Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act ended the system in 1976. Many tharavads were sold; some became heritage hotels and film sets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why Kerala's women had unusual status and property rights historically.
spotlights.memory_hook: The house belonged to the women; the uncle kept the keys.

spotlights.name: The Gulf economy
spotlights.spot_it: Big houses with locked gates in villages, airport crowds before Eid and Onam, and money-transfer shops in every town.
spotlights.story_md: From the 1970s millions of Malayalis worked in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain. Their remittances built Kerala's houses, hospitals and consumer boom: in 2012 Kerala alone received about **16% of all remittances to India**. Malappuram district has the highest share of migrant households. The flows are changing: Gulf numbers fell after 2015 and during COVID-19, and students heading west are now a growing share of emigrants. Kerala even has a department, **NORKA**, for non-resident Keralites.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Remittances are worth around a fifth of Kerala's economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kerala's biggest export is Malayalis.

spotlights.name: Football madness
spotlights.when: Sevens football since the mid-20th century
spotlights.spot_it: Giant cutouts of Messi, Ronaldo and Neymar in rivers and paddy fields during World Cups; floodlit seven-a-side tournaments on dirt grounds.
spotlights.story_md: Malabar is football country. Its own format, **sevens football**, is played on temporary grounds with bamboo stands, foreign players and big crowds. During the 2022 World Cup, fans in Kozhikode set up giant cutouts of Messi, Neymar and Ronaldo in the **Pullavoor river**, and FIFA posted the photo. The Kerala state team has won the **Santosh Trophy** seven times, and **Kerala Blasters** in the Indian Super League draws some of India's biggest football crowds in Kochi. Legend I. M. Vijayan, from Thrissur, once sold soda at the stadium where he later played.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Kerala's outward-looking identity: loyalties to Argentina and Brazil as fierce as to any local team.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Malabar the World Cup happens in the river.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's famous names are disproportionately writers, actors, singers, reformers and public servants. A few who changed India beyond the state:

**K. R. Narayanan**, India's first Dalit President. **Verghese Kurien**, the Kozhikode-born engineer who made India the world's largest milk producer. **M. T. Vasudevan Nair** (1933 to 2024), novelist and screenwriter, Jnanpith 1995, whose death on 25 December 2024 brought the state to a halt. **Arundhati Roy**, who put Kottayam's Ayemenem on the world literary map. And the superstars of Malayalam cinema and music, an industry that is small by Indian standards and admired far beyond it for its realism.

Malayalam cinema produces some 200 films a year. Its actor **Prem Nazir** holds a record for playing the lead in over 700 films, and **Resul Pookutty** from Kerala won an Oscar for sound mixing on Slumdog Millionaire.

spotlights.name: K. R. Narayanan
spotlights.spot_it: A soft-spoken man in glasses: India's tenth President, 1997 to 2002.
spotlights.story_md: Born into a poor Dalit family in a thatched hut in Uzhavoor, Narayanan walked many kilometres to school and, by his own account, sometimes stood outside the classroom because the fees were unpaid. He topped his university in English, studied at the London School of Economics under Harold Laski, joined the foreign service, became ambassador to China and the United States, and was elected **President of India in 1997**, the first from a Dalit community. He was the first President to vote in a general election while in office.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was proof that Kerala's schools could lift a child from a hut to the highest office.
spotlights.memory_hook: From standing outside the classroom to Rashtrapati Bhavan.

spotlights.name: Verghese Kurien
spotlights.spot_it: An engineer with glasses, remembered at Amul's Anand plant as the 'milkman of India'.
spotlights.story_md: Kurien was born in **Kozhikode** on 26 November 1921, trained as a mechanical and metallurgical engineer and was sent, almost against his will, to a government creamery in Anand, Gujarat. He stayed, built the farmer-owned **Amul** cooperative, and as head of the National Dairy Development Board ran **Operation Flood** from 1970, which made India the **world's largest milk producer** by 1998. His birthday is National Milk Day. He famously said he did not like drinking milk.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Malayali led India's White Revolution.
spotlights.memory_hook: The milkman of India did not drink milk.

spotlights.name: Arundhati Roy
spotlights.spot_it: A writer with short curly hair; her novel's world is a riverside house in a Kottayam village.
spotlights.story_md: Roy spent her childhood in **Ayemenem**, near Kottayam, where her mother Mary Roy later won a 1986 Supreme Court case giving Syrian Christian women equal inheritance rights. Her first novel, **The God of Small Things**, set in Ayemenem around a forbidden love across caste lines, won the **Booker Prize in 1997**, the first for a non-expatriate Indian citizen. She then turned to political essays. Her 2025 memoir *Mother Mary Comes to Me* returned to her mother and to Kerala.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made a Kerala village and its caste lines part of world literature.
spotlights.memory_hook: Small things, big prize, one village.

spotlights.name: Mohanlal and Mammootty
spotlights.spot_it: Two actors who have shared Malayalam cinema's top billing for more than four decades.
spotlights.story_md: **Mammootty** (born 1951), a former lawyer, has won three National Awards for best actor and acted in more than 400 films. **Mohanlal** (born 1960) also has 400-plus films, five National Awards and an honorary Lieutenant Colonel's rank in the Territorial Army. His thriller **Drishyam** (2013) was remade in five languages and in Chinese. In September 2025 he was named for the **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** for 2023, India's highest film honour, and his **L2: Empuraan** was 2025's top-grossing Malayalam film.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They carried Malayalam cinema from a regional industry to a national one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two men, eight hundred films, one small industry.

spotlights.name: K. J. Yesudas
spotlights.spot_it: A singer always dressed in white, with a white beard; his voice is the sound of Malayalam film songs since the 1960s.
spotlights.story_md: Yesudas, born to a Latin Catholic family in Fort Kochi, trained in Carnatic music and sang his first film song in 1961. He has recorded tens of thousands of songs in many Indian languages and won the **National Award for best male playback singer eight times**, a record. His recording of **Harivarasanam** is played every night at Sabarimala as the shrine closes. Yet as a non-Hindu he has never been allowed inside the Guruvayur temple, whose deity he has sung about all his life.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His voice is shared by all of Kerala's communities.
spotlights.memory_hook: His lullaby puts a god to sleep each night.

spotlights.name: P. T. Usha
spotlights.spot_it: A sprinter from a fishing village, nicknamed the 'Payyoli Express'.
spotlights.story_md: At the **1984 Los Angeles Olympics**, Usha finished fourth in the 400 m hurdles, missing bronze by **one hundredth of a second**. She won 4 golds and a silver at the 1986 Asian Games in Seoul and over a hundred international medals in all. Her academy in Koyilandy has trained athletes who later competed at the Olympics. In December 2022 she became the first woman president of the **Indian Olympic Association**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made athletics a dream for Indian girls.
spotlights.memory_hook: One hundredth of a second from bronze.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's tourism slogan, **'God's Own Country'**, has run since 1989 and is among India's best known. It sells a short list of experiences: a night on a houseboat in Alappuzha, tea country in Munnar, wildlife at Thekkady, Ayurveda, beaches at Kovalam and Varkala, and old Kochi. The state is small enough to see a great deal in a week, but roads are slow and crowded, and trains along the coast are often faster.

The backwaters are best between September and March. Munnar is cool all year. The monsoon (June to August) is cheap, wet and green, and is the traditional season for Ayurvedic treatment.

spotlights.name: Fort Kochi and its Chinese nets
spotlights.when: Nets thought to date from the 14th or 15th century
spotlights.spot_it: Huge cantilevered fishing nets on teak frames at the harbour mouth, lowered and raised by teams of men using stone counterweights.
spotlights.story_md: The **Chinese fishing nets** (cheena vala) of Fort Kochi are shore-operated lift nets about 10 m high. A team of four to six men walks along the beam to lower the net into the water, then shifts rope-hung stones to raise it with the catch. Tradition credits Chinese traders of the 14th century; others think the Portuguese brought them from Macau. Behind them lies a town of Portuguese, Dutch and British buildings, and **Aspinwall House**, the old trading warehouse that hosts the **Kochi-Muziris Biennale**, India's biggest contemporary art show, held since 2012.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Fort Kochi shows five centuries of foreign trade on one walk.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fishing by seesaw at the mouth of the harbour.

spotlights.name: Periyar and Thekkady
spotlights.spot_it: A lake full of drowned tree stumps, with wild elephants at the water's edge and boats of tourists watching them.
spotlights.story_md: Periyar Lake is not natural. It was created in **1895** by the **Mullaperiyar Dam**, built by the British to send water east through a tunnel to the dry plains of Madurai in Tamil Nadu. The flooded forest left the stumps you still see. Around it is **Periyar Tiger Reserve**, home to elephants, gaur, tigers and lion-tailed macaques, run with the help of former poachers employed as guides. The 130-year-old dam is still operated by Tamil Nadu, and Kerala worries about its safety: one of India's longest inter-state disputes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reserve built on a reservoir, and a dam two states still argue about.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Kerala lake that waters Tamil Nadu.

sections.title: How Kerala earns
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's economy rests on four legs: **remittances**, **services** (trade, tourism, health, education, IT), **plantation crops**, and a growing **ports and shipbuilding** cluster. Services make up about 63% of output and farming less than a tenth. Kerala's GSDP per person, about **₹3.2 lakh** in 2025-26 by state estimates, is well above India's average.

The hill crops are national in scale. Kerala grows most of India's **natural rubber** and **small cardamom**, and much of its pepper, coffee and tea from the Ghats. Kollam processes most of India's export cashew. On the coast, the state built India's **first technology park** (1990), the world's **first fully solar-powered airport** (2015), and its shipyard built India's first home-made aircraft carrier.

The weakness is jobs. Educated youth unemployment is among India's highest, industry is small, and the state borrows heavily to pay pensions and salaries.

spotlights.name: Cardamom and rubber
spotlights.spot_it: Pale green pods at the base of a tall leafy plant under forest shade; white latex dripping into a cup tied to a slashed tree.
spotlights.story_md: **Small cardamom**, the 'queen of spices', is native to the Western Ghats, and Kerala's **Idukki** district grows most of India's crop under forest shade. **Rubber** came from Brazil via the British in the early 1900s and now covers the midland hills of Kottayam and Pathanamthitta; Kerala accounts for most of India's natural rubber, and the **Rubber Board** sits in Kottayam. Tappers start before dawn, when latex flows best. Both crops swing with world prices, and many small growers live on the edge of those swings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Plantation crops tie Kerala's villages to global commodity markets.
spotlights.memory_hook: Queen of spices up the hill, white gold in the midlands.

spotlights.name: Cochin International Airport
spotlights.spot_it: Fields of solar panels beside the runway of a busy international airport.
spotlights.story_md: CIAL was the first Indian airport built as a public-private company, in 1999, with money from thousands of non-resident Malayalis, many of them Gulf workers who wanted a closer airport home. In **August 2015** it became the **world's first airport fully powered by solar energy**, producing as much electricity as it uses from panels spread over its land, some of them over farms growing organic vegetables underneath. The UN Environment Programme gave it its Champions of the Earth award in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Built by migrants, powered by the sun.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Gulf paid for it; the sun runs it.

spotlights.name: INS Vikrant
spotlights.spot_it: A grey aircraft carrier with a ski-jump bow, built in a Kochi dry dock.
spotlights.story_md: **INS Vikrant**, 262 m long and about 45,000 tonnes, is the first aircraft carrier designed and built in India. **Cochin Shipyard**, a public-sector yard founded in 1972, built it over more than a decade and handed it to the Navy, which commissioned it on **2 September 2022**. It carries MiG-29K fighters and helicopters. The yard also builds ships for Europe and Kochi's electric Water Metro boats, a ferry network that opened in 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It put Kochi among the few places in the world that have built a carrier.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's first home-built carrier came out of a Kerala dry dock.

sections.title: Floods, landslides and a virus: living with risk
sections.intro_md:
Kerala's rain and slopes make it beautiful and dangerous. Its hills have been cut for plantations, roads, quarries and houses, and its rivers hemmed in by building. When extreme rain falls, as climate change makes more likely, the water and the hills move.

It has also faced new diseases, partly because it is a global place. India's first **COVID-19** case was a Kerala student back from Wuhan, confirmed on 30 January 2020. In 2018 a **Nipah virus** outbreak in Kozhikode killed 17 people, including the nurse **Lini Puthussery**, before it was contained; the state's response was later turned into the film *Virus* (2019). Kerala's public health system and its tradition of local self-government have made it unusually good at contact tracing and relief.

spotlights.name: The 2018 floods
spotlights.spot_it: Houses flooded to the window line, people on rooftops, fishing boats on city streets.
spotlights.story_md: In August 2018 Kerala had its worst floods in nearly a century. Heavy rain filled reservoirs, and **35 of its 54 dams** were opened, all five shutters of the Idukki dam at once for the first time. About **483 people** died and more than a million stayed in relief camps; Kochi airport shut for two weeks. The heroes were **fishermen** from Kollam and Thiruvananthapuram, who brought 669 boats on lorries and rescued more than **65,000 people**. The state later called them 'Kerala's own army'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It forced a rethink of dam management and building on floodplains.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the state went under, the fishermen came by lorry.

spotlights.name: The Wayanad landslides
spotlights.spot_it: A green valley torn open by a brown scar of mud and boulders; a temporary steel bridge across the river.
spotlights.story_md: In the early hours of **30 July 2024**, after more than 500 mm of rain in two days, the hills above **Mundakkai**, **Chooralmala** and **Punchirimattom** in Meppadi panchayat collapsed. A torrent of mud and boulders swept through villages and a school. More than **400 people** died and many were never found, making it Kerala's worst landslide disaster. The Army's engineers threw a **Bailey bridge** across the river in about a day and a half to reach the cut-off side. Rebuilding the survivors' homes in a new township has been slow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how exposed Kerala's hill settlements are as rainfall becomes more extreme.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole village slid away before dawn.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**2 May 2025.** Prime Minister Modi opened **Vizhinjam International Seaport** near Thiruvananthapuram, India's first deep-water transshipment port. Some of the largest container ships in the world now call there.

**24 May 2025.** The monsoon reached Kerala eight days early, the earliest onset since 2009.

**November 2025.** The LDF government declared Kerala free of extreme poverty, the target of a programme begun in 2021. Critics questioned the survey behind it.

**March 2026.** Attukal Pongala drew a reported 40 lakh women.

**9 April to 4 May 2026.** The Congress-led **UDF won 102 of 140 seats**, ending ten years of LDF rule; the LDF won 35 and the BJP-led NDA 3. **V. D. Satheesan** was sworn in as the 13th Chief Minister on **18 May 2026**. Pinarayi Vijayan became Leader of the Opposition, and India no longer had a state run by the Left.

**25 August 2026.** Kerala officially became **Keralam**.

**September 2026.** The Nehru Trophy race ran on Punnamada Lake, and WikiConference India 2026 met in Kochi.

spotlights.name: Vizhinjam port
spotlights.spot_it: Giant container ships with stacked boxes moored at a long new breakwater, automated cranes above them.
spotlights.story_md: Vizhinjam has a natural depth of about **24 m**, close to the coast and only about 10 nautical miles from the main east-west shipping lane between Europe and the Far East. That lets it take the world's biggest container ships without much dredging, so cargo that used to be transshipped at Colombo, Singapore or Dubai can be handled in India. The first container ship docked in July 2024; the port opened formally on **2 May 2025**. It is operated by Adani Ports for the Kerala government, and it is India's first semi-automated port.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It could change where India's sea cargo changes ships.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fishing village's deep water is now India's front door to the shipping lane.

spotlights.name: The 2026 election
spotlights.spot_it: Results-day crowds in green, red and saffron flags outside counting centres; 'the last Left citadel falls' in the headlines.
spotlights.story_md: Kerala has voted out its government almost every five years since 1977. In 2021 Pinarayi Vijayan's LDF broke that pattern and won a second term. In 2026 the pattern returned with force: the UDF won **102 of 140 seats**, the LDF **35** and the NDA **3**. **V. D. Satheesan**, a lawyer and Paravur MLA since 2001 who had been Leader of the Opposition, became Chief Minister on 18 May 2026. For the first time since 1977, no Indian state had a Left-led government.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It closed a chapter of Indian communism that began in Kerala in 1957.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born in Kerala in 1957, the Left's last state government ended there in 2026.

sections.title: Myth or fact
sections.intro_md:
A few things often said about Kerala, tested.

**'Kerala grows almost all of India's pepper.'** Once true. Older figures say 90% or more, but in recent years Karnataka has produced as much or more. Kerala still dominates cardamom.

**'Kerala elected the world's first communist government.'** Not quite. San Marino had a communist-socialist government from 1945. Kerala's 1957 ministry was among the first elected communist governments in a large democracy.

**'Nangeli cut off her breasts to protest a breast tax.'** A powerful story about the caste tax system of Travancore, but historians have found no contemporary record of Nangeli herself. The taxes on lower castes were real.

**'Kerala is 100% literate.'** It was declared 'totally literate' in 1991 under a campaign standard; the census figure was 94% in 2011.

**'Kerala is God's Own Country because of its temples.'** The phrase is a 1989 tourism slogan.

sections.title: Recap: Kerala in twelve lines
sections.intro_md:
1. A strip 580 km long and at most 120 km wide between the Ghats and the sea; 44 rivers; the monsoon arrives here first.
2. Pepper made it a world port 2,000 years ago: Muziris, the Romans, then Vasco da Gama in 1498.
3. Formed 1 November 1956 from Travancore, Kochi and Malabar; officially **Keralam** since 25 August 2026.
4. 54.7% Hindu, 26.6% Muslim, 18.4% Christian, with Jews and Christians since the first millennium.
5. Reformers broke caste from below: Narayana Guru, Ayyankali, Vaikom, Temple Entry 1936.
6. The Kerala model: literacy 94%, infant deaths a quarter of India's, land reform, Kudumbashree.
7. Malayalam, a classical language; Madhava found pi as an infinite series around 1400.
8. Kathakali, Koodiyattam, Mohiniyattam, theyyam, Kalaripayattu, chenda.
9. Coconut, rice, fish; sadya on a banana leaf; appam and stew; toddy shops.
10. Onam, Vishu, Thrissur Pooram, snake boats, Attukal Pongala.
11. The Gulf built modern Kerala; football is a second religion.
12. Now: Vizhinjam port, a UDF government under V. D. Satheesan, and a new old name.

best_facts.fact: Around 1400, Madhava of Sangamagrama, a Kerala astronomer, wrote pi as an infinite series, about 270 years before Leibniz and Gregory published it in Europe.
best_facts.why_surprising: Calculus-style mathematics in a Kerala village, centuries early.

best_facts.fact: In 1750 the king of Travancore gave his entire kingdom to the god Padmanabha and ruled as the god's servant. The temple's vaults, opened in 2011, held treasure widely estimated at over ₹1 lakh crore, and one vault is still sealed.
best_facts.why_surprising: A god owns the gold and one door has never been opened.

best_facts.fact: Attukal Pongala in Thiruvananthapuram holds the Guinness record for the largest gathering of women: 2.5 million in 2009.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole city becomes a kitchen for one day.

best_facts.fact: Vasco da Gama, whose 1498 landing began European power in India, died in Kochi on Christmas Eve 1524 and was first buried there.
best_facts.why_surprising: The man who opened the sea route ended his life on the coast he reached.

best_facts.fact: In Kuttanad, farmers grow rice 1 to 2 m below sea level on reclaimed lake bed.
best_facts.why_surprising: Kerala farmed below the sea long before the Dutch comparison became a cliché.

best_facts.fact: During the 2018 floods, fishermen brought 669 boats on lorries and rescued more than 65,000 people.
best_facts.why_surprising: A fishing community out-rescued the state.

best_facts.fact: Kerala's Theyyam performers, usually from Dalit communities, become gods for a night, and upper-caste landlords bow to them for blessings.
best_facts.why_surprising: Caste turned upside down, by ritual, every season.

best_facts.fact: The first book ever printed with Malayalam letters was printed in Amsterdam: Hortus Malabaricus, a 12-volume Latin botany of Kerala begun in 1678.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Dutch botany book was Malayalam's first print.

best_facts.fact: A full Koodiyattam play can take up to 41 nights, because the actor elaborates every word.
best_facts.why_surprising: The slowest theatre on Earth is still performed.

best_facts.fact: Cochin International Airport, partly funded by thousands of Gulf migrants, became the world's first fully solar-powered airport in 2015.
best_facts.why_surprising: Migrant money and sunshine run an international airport.

best_facts.fact: Neelakurinji, a shrub of the Munnar hills, flowers en masse once every 12 years and turns the slopes blue; the next bloom is due around 2030.
Verghese Kurien, born in Kozhikode, made India the world's largest milk producer, and said he did not like drinking milk.
best_facts.why_surprising: The milkman of India skipped the milk.

best_facts.fact: Kathakali actors put a seed in their eyes to turn them red for the performance.
best_facts.why_surprising: The famous stare is made, not born.

best_facts.fact: P. T. Usha missed an Olympic bronze in 1984 by one hundredth of a second.
best_facts.why_surprising: The smallest margin in Indian sports memory.

best_facts.fact: Periyar Lake at Thekkady is a reservoir made in 1895 by a dam that sends Kerala's water to Tamil Nadu, and the two states still argue about it.
best_facts.why_surprising: A wildlife lake that is also a water treaty.

best_facts.fact: Yesudas's Harivarasanam closes Sabarimala every night, yet as a Christian he is not allowed inside Guruvayur temple.
India's first COVID-19 case was confirmed in Kerala on 30 January 2020: a student back from Wuhan.
best_facts.why_surprising: A global state catches global things first.

side_dish.title: Why the monsoon starts in Kerala
side_dish.body_md:
Every summer India's weather service announces one date that the whole country waits for: the **onset of the monsoon over Kerala**. Normally it is around **1 June**. In 2025 it came on 24 May.

The reason is geometry. In summer the land of the subcontinent heats far faster than the ocean. Hot air rises over the land, pressure falls, and moist air from the Indian Ocean is pulled in. The winds cross the equator, are bent by Earth's spin and arrive from the **south-west**. Kerala, at India's south-western tip, is the first land they meet.

Then the **Western Ghats** do the rest. The mountains stand 1,000 to 2,600 m high, only 50 to 100 km from the sea. The moist air is forced up, cools and dumps its water: this is **orographic rain**. That is why Kerala gets about 3,000 mm a year while Tamil Nadu, just over the Ghats in the rain shadow, gets far less in the same season.

The monsoon then works north up the coast and across India over about six weeks, reaching the north-west by early July. A late or weak onset in Kerala can mean a poor harvest for the whole country, which is why a forecast for one small state makes national news.

offline_task.title: Make avial, the sadya's mixed vegetable dish
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 3. 35 minutes.**

**Vegetables (about 3 cups, cut into finger-length batons):** raw banana, carrot, drumstick, yam or potato, ash gourd or cucumber, beans.

**Paste:** grind half a cup of grated coconut with 1 teaspoon cumin, 2 green chillies and 2 shallots to a coarse paste with very little water.

**Finish:** half a cup of thick, slightly sour curd, 1 tablespoon coconut oil, a sprig of curry leaves, salt, a pinch of turmeric.

1. Cook the hard vegetables first (yam, banana, carrot, drumstick) with turmeric, salt and half a cup of water, covered, for 8 to 10 minutes. Add the soft ones and cook 5 more minutes. They should hold their shape.
2. Stir in the coconut paste and cook 3 minutes, gently.
3. Turn off the heat. Fold in the beaten curd.
4. Pour raw coconut oil over the top and add curry leaves crushed in your hand. Cover for 5 minutes. Do not stir hard.

Eat it with rice. Notice that it is not a curry with gravy: it should be thick enough to sit on a banana leaf without running. Legend says Bhima invented it when he had to feed guests from leftover vegetables.
